name: Light Glaucous-Blue
lede: Light Glaucous-Blue is a pale, dusty blue-grey from Ridgway's 1912 atlas; our library computes its nearest 1955 ISCC-NBS block, but the 1955 dictionary itself does not list this exact name.

sections.title: A Ridgway tone, not refiled in 1955
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* carries this swatch on plate XXXIV, hue 43″″, tone d [1]. Unlike its sibling [[light-dull-glaucous-blue]], the exact name "Light Glaucous-Blue" does not appear in the 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary; our library's computed nearest block there is 154, "light greenish gray", a calculated match rather than a historical filing [2]. The name builds "light" onto [[grey-teal]], after the dusty, waxy bloom called glaucous [1].

In our color library its closest neighbor is, again, its own sibling [[light-dull-glaucous-blue]], about 3.3 units away, close enough that the two could pass for the same color [3]. [[opal]] sits 3.5 units off and greener, and [[pale-sea-grey]] and Pale Dull Glaucous-Blue both 4.4 units off and lighter [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive of 23,781 paintings matches this tone in 274 of them, about 1.15 percent, as photographed, more common than 69 percent of the named colors we track [4]. It peaks in the 1800s, present in 98 of the 8,345 paintings from that century, 1.4 times the rate its museums' own baseline would predict [4].

Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 53 percent of its 186 clearly-ranked appearances [4]. Alfred Sisley favors it most, in 4 of his 50 works here, 4.3 times his museums' baseline rate, and it shares canvases with Pale Olive Grey more than chance, a lift of 5.4 [4]. The earliest dated match is 1433, in a painting by Robert Campin, 479 years before the name's first 1912 record, so this is a look-alike hue in an old photograph, not proof of the name's age [4]. The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first.
